# Unit 3: Foundations of health communication

Good medicines fail when the message about them fails. Health communication is the sharing of information, feelings and decisions between patients, carers, health workers and the public so that people can protect and improve their health. This unit explains the parts of the communication process, the main models, the types of communication used in healthcare, what blocks it, and the core skills of listening, questioning and empathy, delivered in a way that respects every patient's culture and needs.

## 3.1 Communication: meaning and importance

**Communication** is the process of sending and receiving messages — facts, ideas, feelings — so that they are understood. The word comes from the Latin *communicare*, "to share" or "to make common". Communication is complete only when the receiver understands the message as the sender meant it.

**Health communication** uses communication to inform and influence decisions that improve health — from a one-to-one counselling session to a national vaccination campaign.

**Why communication matters in healthcare**

- Accurate history-taking and assessment depend on it.
- Patients follow treatment they understand and agree with (adherence).
- It prevents medication errors between team members.
- It reduces patient anxiety and builds trust.
- It supports informed consent and patient rights.
- Poor communication is a major cause of complaints and legal action.

## 3.2 Elements of communication

| Element | Meaning | Pharmacy example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sender (source) | The person who starts the message | Pharmacist |
| Message | The information, idea or feeling | "Take this antibiotic for the full seven days" |
| Encoding | Turning the idea into words, signs or symbols | Choosing simple words and a demonstration |
| Channel (medium) | The route the message travels | Face-to-face talk, label, leaflet, phone, video call |
| Receiver | The person who gets the message | Patient or carer |
| Decoding | The receiver interpreting the message | The patient understanding "full seven days" |
| Feedback | The receiver's response, showing what was understood | Patient repeats the instructions back |
| Noise | Anything that distorts the message | Crowd, jargon, pain, worry, accent |
| Context | The setting — physical, social, cultural, emotional | A busy counter versus a private counselling room |

```text
          encodes                 channel                 decodes
 SENDER ----------> MESSAGE ======================> RECEIVER
   ^                          ~~~ NOISE ~~~             |
   |                                                    |
   +-------------------- FEEDBACK <---------------------+
                     (all inside a CONTEXT)
```

**The 7 Cs of effective communication** — clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous.

## 3.3 Models of communication

### Linear models (one-way)

**Shannon and Weaver model (1949)** — developed for telephone signals: information source → transmitter → channel (with noise) → receiver → destination. It introduced the idea of **noise** but has no feedback. A printed label or a mass advertisement works in a mainly linear way.

**Berlo's SMCR model (1960)** — Source, Message, Channel, Receiver. Each part has factors that affect communication:

| Source and Receiver | Message | Channel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system, culture | Content, elements, treatment (how it is arranged), structure, code (language) | The five senses: hearing, seeing, touching, smelling, tasting |

The model stresses that sender and receiver communicate best when their skills, knowledge and culture are similar.

### Interactive model

**Schramm's model (1954)** — communication is two-way. Both people encode, decode and interpret, and understanding happens where their **fields of experience** overlap. Feedback is included. The bigger the overlap, the better the understanding — which is why medical jargon fails with lay patients.

### Transactional model

**Barnlund's transactional model (1970)** — both people send and receive messages **at the same time**, verbal and non-verbal, and are shaped by context, relationship and past experience. While the pharmacist speaks, the patient's frown is already a message. This is the most realistic model for face-to-face healthcare.

### Models used specifically in healthcare consultations

- **Calgary–Cambridge guide** — a structure for consultations: initiating the session → gathering information → physical examination (where relevant) → explanation and planning → closing the session, with "providing structure" and "building the relationship" running throughout.
- **Patient-centred communication** — exploring the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations (often shortened to ICE), finding common ground and sharing decisions.

| Model type | Direction | Feedback | Best example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Linear | One-way | None | Label, poster, broadcast |
| Interactive | Two-way, turn by turn | Yes | Phone call, email exchange |
| Transactional | Two-way, simultaneous | Continuous | Face-to-face counselling |

## 3.4 Types of communication

### By form

| Form | Description | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verbal (oral) | Spoken words | Counselling, phone calls, ward rounds |
| Written | Words on paper or screen | Labels, prescriptions, leaflets, case notes, emails |
| Non-verbal | Messages without words | Facial expression, eye contact, posture, gestures, touch, distance |
| Paraverbal | How words are spoken | Tone, pitch, speed, volume, pauses |
| Visual | Images and symbols | Pictograms, charts, videos, demonstration |

**Non-verbal communication (body language)** often carries feelings more strongly than words. When words and body language disagree, people tend to believe the body language.

- **Kinesics** — body movements, gestures, facial expressions, posture.
- **Oculesics** — eye contact.
- **Proxemics** — use of space: intimate (very close), personal (about arm's length), social and public distances. Counselling usually happens at personal-to-social distance.
- **Haptics** — touch; use with care and respect for culture and gender.
- **Chronemics** — use of time; keeping someone waiting sends a message.
- **Appearance** — clean, professional dress builds confidence.

### By number of people involved

**1. Intrapersonal** — talking to oneself (self-talk). Important in coping and stress.

**2. Interpersonal communication** — between two people or a very small number, face-to-face or by phone. Examples: pharmacist–patient counselling, pharmacist–doctor discussion. Features: immediate feedback, personal, can be adapted to the listener. The quality of interpersonal communication decides trust and adherence.

**3. Group communication** — among three or more people with a shared purpose. Examples: a patient education session for diabetics, a ward team meeting, a support group. Features: more ideas and support, but needs a leader, turn-taking and a clear goal; quiet members may not speak.

**4. Mass communication** — one source reaching very large audiences through media: television, radio, newspapers, posters, social media. Examples: national campaigns on immunisation, tobacco control, tuberculosis and anaemia. Features: wide reach and low cost per person, but little feedback and no tailoring; best for awareness, less for changing personal behaviour on its own.

**5. Telehealth communication** — providing health services and information at a distance using technology.

| Form of telehealth | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Real-time (synchronous) | Video or voice consultation |
| Store-and-forward (asynchronous) | Sending photos or reports for later review |
| Remote monitoring | Home blood pressure or glucose readings sent to a clinic |
| Mobile health (mHealth) | SMS reminders, health apps, WhatsApp-based follow-up |

In India, the Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (2020) set rules for doctors consulting remotely. The national eSanjeevani service provides free online consultations, and Tele-MANAS provides tele-mental-health support.

**Advantages of telehealth:** reaches rural and remote patients, saves travel and time, useful for follow-up and chronic disease, reduces infection spread.

**Limits and good practice:** no physical examination; poor network and devices; difficulty reading body language; privacy risks; some older people struggle with technology. Good practice: confirm the patient's identity, ensure a private setting, speak clearly, check understanding more often, document the consultation and protect data.

### By direction (inside an organisation)

- **Downward** — from senior to junior (instructions, policies).
- **Upward** — from junior to senior (reports, suggestions, error reporting).
- **Horizontal (lateral)** — between people at the same level or between departments (pharmacist to nurse).
- **Formal** (official channels) and **informal** (grapevine) communication.

## 3.5 Barriers to effective communication in clinical settings

A **barrier** is anything that stops, distorts or delays a message.

| Barrier | Examples in clinical settings | How to reduce it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical / environmental | Noise, crowding, no privacy at the counter, glass screen, poor lighting | Counselling area, reduce noise, face the patient |
| Physiological | Pain, hearing loss, poor vision, speech problems, fatigue, illness, effects of medicines | Speak clearly, use large print, hearing aids, return when the patient is comfortable |
| Psychological / emotional | Fear, anxiety, anger, denial, depression, embarrassment | Calm approach, reassurance, empathy, privacy |
| Semantic / language | Jargon ("hypertension", "PRN", "bd"), different language, words with two meanings | Plain language, local language, interpreter, check understanding |
| Cultural | Beliefs about illness, gender norms, taboos, different meanings of gestures | Cultural awareness, respect, ask rather than assume |
| Health literacy | Difficulty reading or using health information, poor numeracy | Pictograms, demonstrations, teach-back |
| Attitudinal | Prejudice, stereotyping, superiority, impatience, lack of interest | Respect, non-judgemental attitude, self-awareness |
| Organisational / system | Heavy workload, short time, poor handover, rigid hierarchy, unclear roles | Structured tools, team training, adequate staffing |
| Technological | Poor network, faulty devices, illegible handwriting, e-record errors | Backup methods, clear typed orders, double checks |
| Perceptual | Selective attention, hearing only what one expects | Summarise, repeat key points |

**Barriers created by the professional:** using jargon, talking too fast, interrupting, giving too much information at once, not looking at the patient, writing while the patient speaks, sounding rushed, judging the patient.

## 3.6 Active listening, questioning techniques and empathy

### Hearing and listening

**Hearing** is the passive physical process of sound reaching the ear. **Listening** is the active mental process of attending to, understanding, remembering and responding to the message.

**Types of listening:** discriminative (sounds), informational (facts), critical (judging content), empathetic (understanding feelings) and appreciative (enjoyment).

### Active listening

**Active listening** means giving full attention to the speaker, understanding both words and feelings, and showing that you have understood.

**Skills of active listening**

| Skill | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Attending | Face the patient, comfortable eye contact, open posture, lean slightly forward, put away distractions |
| Minimal encouragers | Nods, "I see", "go on", "mm-hm" |
| Paraphrasing | Repeat the content in your own words: "So the cough wakes you at night" |
| Reflecting feelings | Name the emotion: "You sound worried about the side effects" |
| Clarifying | "When you say dizzy, do you mean the room spins?" |
| Summarising | Pull the main points together at the end |
| Silence | Allow pauses so the patient can think and continue |
| Not interrupting | Let the patient finish |

The **SOLER** reminder for attending posture: **S**it squarely facing the patient, **O**pen posture, **L**ean slightly forward, **E**ye contact, **R**elaxed manner.

**Blocks to listening:** planning your reply while the other speaks, judging, giving advice too early, interrupting, daydreaming, being distracted by noise or the phone, and filtering (hearing only what you want).

### Questioning techniques

| Type of question | Purpose | Example | Use carefully because |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Open | Invites a full answer; gathers information and feelings | "How have you been taking these tablets?" | Talkative patients may wander |
| Closed | Gets a specific fact, often yes/no | "Are you allergic to penicillin?" | Gives little detail |
| Probing | Explores further | "Tell me more about the rash" | Can feel intrusive |
| Clarifying | Removes doubt | "What do you mean by 'often'?" | — |
| Reflective | Turns the patient's words back | "You feel the medicine isn't working?" | — |
| Leading | Suggests the expected answer | "You take it after food, don't you?" | Patient may agree to please you — avoid |
| Multiple (stacked) | Several questions at once | "Do you smoke, drink, and take other medicines?" | Confusing — avoid |
| Hypothetical | Explores "what if" | "What would you do if you missed a dose?" | — |

**Funnel technique** — start with broad open questions, then narrow to specific closed questions to confirm details.

**The three prime questions** used in patient counselling (from the Indian Health Service model):

1. What did the doctor tell you the medicine is for?
2. How did the doctor tell you to take it?
3. What did the doctor tell you to expect?

These find out what the patient already knows so the pharmacist fills the gaps.

### Empathy

**Empathy** is the ability to understand another person's feelings and point of view as if from their position, and to communicate that understanding — "walking in their shoes" while remaining yourself.

| Empathy | Sympathy | Apathy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feeling *with* the person | Feeling *for* (pity) the person | No concern |
| "It sounds frightening to start insulin" | "Oh, poor you" | "That's the rule" |
| Keeps professional balance; patient feels understood | Can feel patronising; may focus on the helper's feelings | Damages trust |

**Components of empathy:** cognitive (understanding), emotional (sharing the feeling) and compassionate (wanting to help). Empathy is shown through attentive listening, reflecting feelings, a warm tone and appropriate non-verbal behaviour.

**Benefits:** greater patient satisfaction and trust, more information shared, better adherence, less anxiety.

## 3.7 Culturally appropriate and inclusive communication

**Culture** is the shared beliefs, values, language, customs and behaviour of a group. India's diversity of language, religion, region, caste and economic background makes cultural sensitivity essential.

**Cultural competence** is the ability to communicate and provide care effectively to people from different cultures. It grows through:

- **Awareness** of one's own beliefs and biases
- **Knowledge** of other cultures' health beliefs and practices
- **Skill** in adapting communication
- **Respect** and a genuine wish to understand

**Practical guidance**

1. Use the patient's preferred language; use trained interpreters rather than children or untrained relatives for important information.
2. Ask about beliefs: "What do you think caused this?", "Are you taking any home or traditional remedies?"
3. Respect religious practice — fasting (Ramadan, Navratri) may change dosing times; some patients avoid gelatin or alcohol-containing products.
4. Respect gender preferences; some patients prefer a professional of the same gender.
5. Be careful with touch, eye contact and gestures, which carry different meanings in different cultures.
6. Avoid stereotypes; treat each person as an individual.

**Inclusive communication** means making sure everyone can access and understand information, whatever their ability, age, literacy, gender identity or background.

| Group | Inclusive practice |
| --- | --- |
| Hearing impairment | Face the person, speak clearly (do not shout), written notes, sign language interpreter |
| Visual impairment | Large print, tactile markers, verbal explanation, identify yourself |
| Low literacy | Pictograms, colour-coded schedules, demonstration, teach-back |
| Children | Age-appropriate words, involve parent, play |
| Elderly | Slower pace, check hearing and vision, involve carer, simple schedules |
| Cognitive or intellectual disability | Short sentences, one idea at a time, visual aids, involve carer |
| Gender and sexual minorities | Respectful, non-assuming language, use preferred name and pronouns, confidentiality |
| People with mental illness | Respect, avoid stigmatising words, patience |

**Plain language rules:** short sentences, common words, active voice, one idea per sentence, explain any medical term, use numbers carefully ("one tablet in the morning and one at night" rather than "bd").

## Remember

- Elements: sender, message, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding, feedback, noise, context.
- Models: Shannon–Weaver (linear, introduced noise), Berlo SMCR, Schramm (interactive, field of experience), Barnlund (transactional, simultaneous). Calgary–Cambridge guide for consultations.
- Types: interpersonal, group, mass, telehealth (real-time, store-and-forward, remote monitoring, mHealth).
- Barriers: physical, physiological, psychological, semantic, cultural, health literacy, attitudinal, organisational, technological.
- Active listening: attend (SOLER), encourage, paraphrase, reflect, clarify, summarise, allow silence.
- Prefer open questions first (funnel technique); avoid leading and multiple questions.
- Empathy = feeling with; sympathy = feeling for.
- Cultural competence = awareness, knowledge, skill, respect; use interpreters, plain language and teach-back.

# Unit 4: Professional communication in healthcare settings

In practice a pharmacist talks to patients, worried relatives, doctors, nurses and administrators, often on the same morning. Some conversations are routine; some carry bad news or strong emotions; all must respect confidentiality and consent, and many must be written down accurately. This unit covers communication with patients, caregivers and teams, breaking difficult news, handling emotional situations, the legal and ethical rules, written records, and digital communication tools.

## 4.1 Communication with patients

**Patient-centred communication** puts the patient's needs, values and preferences at the centre. The professional explains, but also listens and involves the patient in decisions.

**Stages of a pharmacist–patient counselling session**

```text
1. OPENING        greet, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain purpose, ensure privacy
       |
2. GATHERING      what does the patient know? (three prime questions), history, allergies,
       |          other medicines, concerns
3. EXPLAINING     name and purpose of medicine, how and when to take it, what to expect,
       |          common side effects and what to do, storage, missed dose, interactions
4. CHECKING       teach-back: "Tell me how you will take this, so I know I explained it well"
       |
5. CLOSING        summary, written information, invite questions, how to contact the pharmacy
```

**Good practices**

- Use the patient's name and introduce yourself.
- Sit or stand at the patient's level; maintain comfortable eye contact.
- Speak slowly, in plain words, in the patient's language.
- Give the most important points first; limit to a few key messages.
- Demonstrate devices (inhaler, insulin pen, eye drops) and ask the patient to show you.
- Ask about the patient's concerns and expectations.
- Respect the patient's right to make choices.
- Provide written or pictorial information to take home.

**Teach-back method** — the patient explains in their own words what they have been told. If it is wrong, the professional explains again differently and rechecks. It tests the clarity of the explanation, not the patient's intelligence.

## 4.2 Communication with caregivers

**Caregivers** (carers) are family members or others who look after a patient — the parent of a child, the son of an elderly person, the spouse of a stroke patient.

- Caregivers often give medicines, notice side effects and attend appointments, so they need clear instructions too.
- **Respect the patient's confidentiality and autonomy**: share information with a carer only with the patient's consent, except when the patient lacks capacity (young child, unconscious, severe dementia), when the legal guardian or authorised representative is informed.
- Include the patient in the conversation even when a carer is present; do not talk "over" the patient.
- Recognise caregiver stress (burden, exhaustion, guilt); offer support and information about help available.
- Give practical tools: dosing charts, pill organisers, a list of warning signs and whom to call.

## 4.3 Communication within interdisciplinary teams

Healthcare is delivered by teams: doctors, pharmacists, nurses, dieticians, physiotherapists, laboratory staff, social workers. Most serious medication errors involve a breakdown in team communication — illegible orders, verbal orders misheard, incomplete handover.

**Principles of good team communication**

- Know and respect each member's role and expertise.
- Speak up about safety concerns, whatever your position in the hierarchy.
- Be clear, specific and brief; give facts and a recommendation.
- Confirm that the message was received correctly.
- Document what was agreed.

**SBAR — a structured tool** for passing information, for example when a pharmacist phones a doctor about a problem prescription:

| Step | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S – Situation | What is happening now | "I am calling about Mr Rao in bed 12; the prescription has two drugs that interact." |
| B – Background | Relevant history | "He was admitted with pneumonia and is on long-term therapy for epilepsy." |
| A – Assessment | What you think the problem is | "The new antibiotic may raise the level of his anti-epileptic medicine." |
| R – Recommendation | What you suggest | "Please consider an alternative antibiotic, or we can monitor drug levels." |

Variants: **ISBAR** adds **I – Identify** yourself and the patient at the start.

**Other safety techniques**

- **Read-back / repeat-back** — the receiver repeats a verbal or telephone order; the sender confirms it. Spell out drug names and say numbers digit by digit ("one-five, fifteen").
- **Closed-loop communication** — sender gives a message → receiver repeats it → sender confirms → task done and reported.
- **Structured handover** at shift change, using a checklist.
- **Avoid error-prone abbreviations** (such as "U" for units or "µg" written badly) and trailing zeros ("1.0 mg" may be read as 10 mg).
- **Assertive communication** — express concerns clearly and respectfully: "I am concerned this dose is higher than usual; can we check it together?"

**Communication styles**

| Style | Features | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Passive | Avoids conflict, does not express needs | Concerns go unheard; errors continue |
| Aggressive | Blaming, loud, disrespectful | Others become defensive |
| Passive-aggressive | Indirect resentment, sarcasm | Damages trust |
| Assertive | Clear, honest, respectful, firm | Best for teamwork and safety |

## 4.4 Delivering difficult news

**Bad or difficult news** is any information that seriously and negatively changes a person's view of their future — a diagnosis of cancer or HIV, a serious side effect, the need for lifelong treatment, an error that affected the patient, or a death. Diagnoses are given by the doctor, but pharmacists often answer the questions that follow, explain treatment with serious consequences, or disclose errors.

**SPIKES protocol** (Baile and Buckman) — a six-step approach:

| Step | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| S – Setting up | Private room, sit down, switch off phone, enough time, invite a support person if the patient wishes, tissues available |
| P – Perception | Find out what the patient already knows: "What have you been told so far?" |
| I – Invitation | Ask how much the patient wants to know: "Would you like me to explain the details?" |
| K – Knowledge | Give a warning shot ("I'm afraid I have some difficult news"), then information in small pieces, plain words, no jargon; check understanding |
| E – Emotions (with Empathy) | Notice the emotion, name it, allow silence, respond with empathy: "I can see this is a shock" |
| S – Strategy and Summary | Summarise, agree a plan and next steps, offer support and follow-up |

**Do's and don'ts**

| Do | Don't |
| --- | --- |
| Be honest and kind | Give news in a corridor or over a crowded counter |
| Allow silence and tears | Use jargon or euphemisms that confuse |
| Offer hope that is realistic (symptom control, support) | Give false reassurance ("Everything will be fine") |
| Check what was understood | Rush or overload with information |
| Arrange follow-up | Leave the patient alone without a plan |

## 4.5 Handling emotionally charged situations

Patients and relatives may be angry, frightened, grieving or distressed — because of illness, waiting, costs, a medicine being out of stock, or an error.

**De-escalation steps for an angry person**

1. **Stay calm** — keep your voice low and steady; control your own reaction.
2. **Ensure safety** — keep a safe distance; do not block exits; call for help if there is any risk of violence.
3. **Move to privacy** if possible.
4. **Listen fully** without interrupting.
5. **Acknowledge the feeling** — "I can see you're upset that you had to wait so long."
6. **Apologise for the experience** where appropriate, without blaming others.
7. **Find out what is needed** and explain what you can do; offer choices.
8. **Agree on a solution** and follow through; involve a senior if needed.
9. **Document** the incident.

**Responding to other emotions**

- **Anxiety** — reassure with facts, explain step by step, give written information.
- **Grief** — allow silence, show compassion, avoid clichés; practical help with arrangements.
- **Crying** — offer tissues and time; do not rush to stop the tears.
- **Denial** — do not force acceptance at once; give information gradually.
- **Disclosure of an error** — be open and honest, apologise, explain what happened and what will be done to put it right and prevent recurrence; report as per policy.

## 4.6 Legal and ethical issues in health communication

### Ethical principles

| Principle | Meaning | In communication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Autonomy | Respect the person's right to decide | Give full information; respect refusal |
| Beneficence | Act in the patient's best interest | Give advice that helps |
| Non-maleficence | Do no harm | Avoid misleading or frightening information |
| Justice | Fairness and equal treatment | Same quality of communication for every patient |
| Veracity | Truthfulness | Do not deceive the patient |
| Fidelity | Keeping promises and loyalty | Keep confidences, follow up as promised |

### Confidentiality

**Confidentiality** is the duty not to disclose personal health information that a patient shares with a professional, without the patient's permission.

**Why it matters:** patients disclose sensitive information (sexual health, mental illness, substance use) only if they trust it will be protected. Breach damages trust and can cause discrimination.

**Good practice**

- Discuss health matters in a private area, in a low voice.
- Do not discuss patients with friends, family or on social media — even without names, if they could be identified.
- Keep records locked or password-protected; log out of computers; do not leave prescriptions in view.
- Share information only with those directly involved in care, on a need-to-know basis.
- Confirm identity before giving information on the telephone.

**When disclosure may be allowed without consent** (limited and only as much as necessary): when required by law or a court order; when there is a serious risk of harm to the patient or others; mandatory reporting such as notifiable diseases or suspected child sexual abuse (under the POCSO Act); and when the patient lacks capacity and information must go to the legal guardian. Always follow local law and institutional policy and seek senior advice.

**Relevant Indian provisions (outline):** the Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015 of the Pharmacy Council of India describe the professional conduct expected of pharmacists, including respect for patient confidentiality; the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 gives persons with mental illness the right to confidentiality; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the processing of digital personal data.

### Consent

**Consent** is the permission a patient gives for a procedure, treatment or sharing of information. **Informed consent** requires:

1. **Capacity** — the person can understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a decision.
2. **Disclosure** — information about the nature, purpose, benefits, risks and alternatives, including doing nothing.
3. **Understanding** — the person has understood it (check, do not assume).
4. **Voluntariness** — given freely, without pressure or coercion.
5. **Decision** — the person agrees (or refuses) and may withdraw at any time.

| Type of consent | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Implied | Patient holds out an arm for a blood pressure check |
| Verbal (expressed orally) | Patient agrees to a medication review |
| Written | Surgery, clinical trials, high-risk procedures |

**Special situations:** minors (consent usually by parent or guardian, while involving the child), emergencies (treatment necessary to save life may proceed), patients lacking capacity (decision by legal representative in the patient's best interest), and research (written informed consent under ethics committee approval, as required by the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019).

## 4.7 Writing patient records, reports and discharge summaries

### Principles of good documentation

Records are legal documents and a means of communication between professionals.

- **Accurate and factual** — record what was seen, said and done; avoid opinions and labels.
- **Complete** — include all relevant information.
- **Clear and legible** — readable handwriting or typed; standard terms only.
- **Contemporaneous** — written at the time or as soon as possible.
- **Dated, timed and signed** with name and designation.
- **Concise and objective** — "Patient states she missed four doses this week", not "Patient is careless".
- **Corrections** — draw a single line through the error so it stays readable, write the correction, initial and date it; never erase, overwrite or use correction fluid.
- **Confidential** and securely stored.
- "If it was not documented, it was not done."

### SOAP format

Widely used for clinical and pharmacist notes:

| Part | Content | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S – Subjective | What the patient reports: symptoms, history, concerns | "Feels dizzy on standing since the new tablet was started" |
| O – Objective | Measurable findings: vital signs, lab values, medication list | Blood pressure readings, current drugs |
| A – Assessment | The professional's interpretation of the problem | Possible drug-related postural hypotension |
| P – Plan | What will be done: recommendation, monitoring, education, follow-up | Discuss with prescriber; counsel to rise slowly; review in one week |

### Common records and reports in pharmacy

- **Medication history** — current and past medicines, OTC, herbal, allergies, adherence.
- **Medication reconciliation** — comparing the medicines a patient was taking with those ordered at admission, transfer and discharge, and resolving differences.
- **Pharmacist intervention record** — problem found, recommendation made, outcome.
- **Adverse drug reaction report** — suspected reactions reported on the Suspected Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting Form to the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India.
- **Incident or medication error report.**
- **Counselling record.**

### Discharge summary

A **discharge summary** is a written account of a patient's hospital stay, given to the patient and the next care provider so care continues safely.

**Usual contents**

1. Patient details (name, age, sex, hospital number, address)
2. Dates of admission and discharge; name of the consultant and department
3. Diagnosis (final and secondary)
4. Reason for admission and brief history
5. Key examination findings and investigation results
6. Treatment given (medicines, procedures, surgery)
7. Course in hospital and condition at discharge
8. **Discharge medicines** — name, strength, how to take, duration, with changes from pre-admission medicines clearly stated (started, stopped, changed)
9. Allergies and adverse reactions
10. Advice: diet, activity, wound care, warning signs that need urgent return
11. Follow-up appointments and pending results
12. Name, signature and contact of the responsible doctor

The pharmacist's role: reconcile discharge medicines, check for errors, and counsel the patient and carer on the new regimen.

### Writing reports

A professional report has a title, introduction (purpose), method or background, findings, conclusions, recommendations, and the author's name and date. Use headings, short paragraphs, tables where helpful, and neutral factual language.

## 4.8 Use of technology and digital communication tools in healthcare

| Tool | Use | Points to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electronic health records (EHR) | Shared, legible, searchable patient records | Data entry errors, privacy, log out after use |
| Electronic prescribing | Removes handwriting errors, alerts for interactions and allergies | Alert fatigue, wrong selection from drop-down lists |
| Hospital information systems | Link pharmacy, laboratory, wards and billing | Downtime procedures needed |
| Telehealth and telepharmacy | Remote consultation and counselling | Identity check, privacy, documentation |
| Mobile health apps and SMS reminders | Adherence reminders, health education | Reliability of apps, data security |
| Email and messaging | Quick team communication | Professional tone; avoid sending identifiable data on unsecured platforms |
| Social media | Public health messages, professional networking | Never post patient information; keep professional boundaries; avoid spreading unverified claims |
| Clinical decision-support and drug databases | Check doses, interactions | Use as an aid to judgement, not a replacement |
| Barcode scanning | Right drug to the right patient | Do not override without checking |

**National digital health initiatives in India:** the **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission** creates a digital health ecosystem in which each person can have an **ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account)** number linking their health records with consent; **eSanjeevani** offers national telemedicine consultations.

**Digital etiquette for professionals**

- Use official, secure systems for patient information.
- Write messages that are clear, polite and complete; check the recipient before sending.
- Respect consent and privacy in every digital exchange.
- Keep records of advice given remotely.
- Remember that written digital messages are permanent and can be forwarded.

## Remember

- Counselling stages: open → gather → explain → check (teach-back) → close.
- Share information with carers only with consent, unless the patient lacks capacity.
- SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (ISBAR adds Identify). Read-back and closed-loop communication prevent verbal-order errors.
- Assertive is the best style for safety.
- SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions/Empathy, Strategy and Summary.
- De-escalation: stay calm, stay safe, listen, acknowledge, offer options, document.
- Ethics: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice (plus veracity, fidelity).
- Informed consent: capacity, disclosure, understanding, voluntariness, decision; implied, verbal, written.
- Documentation: accurate, complete, legible, contemporaneous, signed; correct with a single line. SOAP = Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.
- Discharge summary must list discharge medicines with all changes clearly marked.
- ABDM gives the ABHA number; eSanjeevani is the national telemedicine service.

# Unit 5: Health psychology and behavioural interventions

Knowing that smoking harms, or that blood pressure tablets must be taken every day, does not by itself make people stop smoking or take their tablets. Health psychology explains why people act as they do about their health and offers tested ways to help them change. This unit covers the health belief model and illness behaviour, the mind–body link and psychosomatic illness, behaviour change theories used to improve treatment adherence, psychological first aid and crisis communication, and how communication can promote mental health and reduce stigma.

## 5.1 Health behaviour

**Health behaviour** is any action a person takes to stay healthy, prevent disease or detect it early — eating well, exercising, using seat belts, getting vaccinated, going for screening.

- **Health-enhancing behaviours** — exercise, balanced diet, adequate sleep, handwashing.
- **Health-compromising behaviours** — smoking, alcohol misuse, unsafe sex, sedentary lifestyle.

Health behaviours depend on knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, habits, emotions, social influence, culture, cost and access.

## 5.2 Health belief model and illness behaviour

### Health belief model (HBM)

The **health belief model** was developed in the 1950s by social psychologists in the US Public Health Service (Hochbaum, Rosenstock and colleagues) to explain why people did not use free tuberculosis screening. It says a person's decision to take a health action depends on their beliefs.

| Component | Meaning | Example: taking blood pressure tablets regularly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Perceived susceptibility | Belief about one's chance of getting the problem | "I could have a stroke" |
| Perceived severity | Belief about how serious the problem would be | "A stroke would leave me disabled" |
| Perceived benefits | Belief that the action will reduce the risk | "Tablets lower my risk" |
| Perceived barriers | Costs, side effects, inconvenience, fear | "They make me tired and cost money" |
| Cues to action | Triggers that prompt action | A relative's stroke, a reminder SMS, a doctor's advice |
| Self-efficacy (added later) | Confidence in one's ability to take the action | "I can remember to take them every morning" |

**Modifying factors:** age, gender, education, culture, personality and knowledge influence these beliefs.

```text
Modifying factors -> perceived susceptibility + severity  = perceived THREAT ----+
(age, culture,                                                                   |
 knowledge)        -> perceived benefits minus barriers                     ---> LIKELIHOOD OF ACTION
                   -> self-efficacy                                         ---+        ^
                                                    cues to action -----------------------+
```

**Using the HBM in counselling:** explain personal risk honestly (susceptibility), explain consequences without terrifying (severity), stress benefits, find and remove barriers (cost, side effects, timing), provide cues (reminders), build confidence.

**Limitations:** assumes people make rational decisions; ignores emotions, habits and social pressure; does not explain how beliefs change over time.

**Theory of planned behaviour (Icek Ajzen)** — another belief-based model: behaviour follows **intention**, which depends on **attitude** towards the behaviour, **subjective norms** (what important others expect) and **perceived behavioural control**.

### Illness behaviour

**Illness behaviour** is the way people perceive, evaluate and respond to symptoms — whether they ignore them, treat themselves, consult someone or seek medical care. The term was introduced by David Mechanic.

**Factors affecting illness behaviour (Mechanic):** how visible and recognisable the symptoms are; how serious they seem; how much they disrupt daily life; how often they occur; tolerance of others; knowledge and cultural beliefs; denial; competing needs (work, family); other explanations for the symptoms; and availability and cost of treatment.

**Stages of illness experience (Suchman)**

| Stage | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Symptom experience | The person notices something is wrong and decides it means illness |
| 2. Assumption of the sick role | Seeks advice from family and friends; may self-treat |
| 3. Medical care contact | Consults a professional for diagnosis and legitimacy |
| 4. Dependent patient role | Accepts treatment and follows the professional's advice |
| 5. Recovery or rehabilitation | Gives up the sick role and returns to normal duties (or adjusts to chronic illness) |

**Sick role (Talcott Parsons)** — rights: exemption from normal duties and from blame. Obligations: wanting to get well and seeking and cooperating with competent help.

**Types of illness behaviour**

- **Appropriate** — seeking help at the right time.
- **Delay** — ignoring serious symptoms through fear, denial or cost (common in cancer and heart disease).
- **Excessive** — frequent consultations for minor symptoms, health anxiety.
- **Self-medication** — common in India; the pharmacist guides responsible self-care and refers when needed.

## 5.3 Psychosomatic illnesses and the mind–body connection

### The mind–body connection

The mind and body continually influence each other. Thoughts and emotions cause changes in the nervous, endocrine and immune systems, and physical illness affects mood and thinking.

**Pathways linking stress and emotion to the body**

```text
Stressor -> brain (appraisal) -> hypothalamus
                                    |
               +--------------------+---------------------+
               |                                          |
  Sympathetic nervous system                 HPA axis: hypothalamus -> pituitary
  -> adrenal medulla -> adrenaline,          -> adrenal cortex -> cortisol
     noradrenaline                                      |
  -> heart rate, BP, blood sugar up          -> immunity suppressed with long exposure,
                                                blood sugar up, healing slowed
```

- **Psychoneuroimmunology** studies how psychological factors affect the immune system through nerves and hormones. Long-term stress is associated with slower wound healing and greater vulnerability to infection.
- **Behavioural pathway** — stressed or depressed people may smoke more, drink, sleep poorly, eat badly and miss medicines.
- **Placebo and nocebo effects** — positive expectations can improve symptoms (placebo); negative expectations can produce side effects (nocebo). This shows why the way a medicine is explained matters.

### Psychosomatic illnesses

**Psychosomatic (psychophysiological) illnesses** are physical conditions in which psychological factors such as stress, anxiety or emotional conflict play an important role in starting or worsening the disease. The physical changes are real, not imagined.

| System | Conditions where psychological factors contribute |
| --- | --- |
| Cardiovascular | Hypertension, coronary heart disease, palpitations |
| Respiratory | Bronchial asthma (attacks triggered by emotion), hyperventilation |
| Gastrointestinal | Irritable bowel syndrome, functional dyspepsia; stress worsens peptic ulcer symptoms (though *Helicobacter pylori* is the main cause) |
| Skin | Psoriasis, eczema, urticaria, acne flares |
| Musculoskeletal | Tension headache, back pain, fibromyalgia |
| Endocrine | Poor control of diabetes under stress |
| Other | Migraine, sleep disturbance, menstrual irregularity |

**Distinguish:** psychosomatic illness = real physical disease worsened by the mind; somatic symptom disorder (Unit 2) = distressing symptoms with excessive worry, often without a full physical explanation; malingering = deliberately faking symptoms for gain.

**Management approach:** treat the physical disease, and also address stress, sleep and mood (relaxation, counselling, exercise, support). The pharmacist reinforces both.

## 5.4 Behaviour change theories in treatment adherence

### Adherence

**Adherence** is the extent to which a person's behaviour — taking medicines, following a diet, changing lifestyle — matches the recommendations agreed with a health professional. The word "adherence" is preferred over "compliance" because it implies the patient's agreement rather than obedience. The World Health Organization has stressed that poor adherence to long-term therapy is a worldwide problem.

| Type of non-adherence | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Primary | Prescription never collected |
| Unintentional | Forgetting, misunderstanding, inability to use a device |
| Intentional | Deciding to stop due to side effects, cost, feeling better or beliefs |

**WHO's five dimensions affecting adherence:** social and economic factors; health system and team factors; condition-related factors; therapy-related factors (complexity, duration, side effects); and patient-related factors (knowledge, beliefs, motivation, memory).

### Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)

**CBT** is a structured, short-term, goal-oriented psychological therapy. Aaron Beck developed cognitive therapy; Albert Ellis developed rational emotive behaviour therapy. Its central idea is that **thoughts, feelings and behaviours are linked**, so changing unhelpful thoughts and behaviours changes feelings.

```text
          THOUGHTS
     "These tablets will damage
        my kidneys"
         /        \
        /          \
   FEELINGS ------ BEHAVIOUR
   fear, worry      skips doses
```

**Ellis's ABC model:** **A**ctivating event → **B**elief about it → **C**onsequence (emotion and behaviour). Changing B changes C.

**Common thinking errors (cognitive distortions):** all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising, overgeneralisation, jumping to conclusions, mental filter (seeing only the negative), "should" statements.

**CBT techniques**

- Identifying automatic negative thoughts
- Challenging them with evidence (cognitive restructuring)
- Behavioural activation (planning rewarding activities, useful in depression)
- Graded exposure (facing fears step by step, used in phobias)
- Problem-solving training
- Relaxation and breathing
- Homework and self-monitoring diaries

**CBT and adherence:** helps patients challenge false beliefs about medicines ("I'll get addicted to inhalers"), solve practical problems (forgetting, timing), and manage the depression and anxiety that reduce adherence. CBT is used for depression, anxiety, insomnia, chronic pain, smoking cessation and weight management. A pharmacist uses CBT-style questions in counselling; formal CBT is delivered by trained therapists.

### Transtheoretical model (TTM) — stages of change

Developed by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente from studies of smokers. It says people change behaviour through stages, and advice should match the stage.

| Stage | Description | What helps (pharmacist's role) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Precontemplation | Not thinking of change in the next six months; may not see a problem | Raise awareness gently; personalised information about risks; do not lecture |
| Contemplation | Thinking of change within six months; weighing pros and cons; ambivalent | Discuss benefits and barriers; build motivation; explore ambivalence |
| Preparation | Intends to act soon (within a month); may have taken small steps | Help set a quit date or plan; discuss options and support |
| Action | Has changed behaviour recently (less than six months) | Encourage, reward, manage withdrawal or side effects, prevent relapse |
| Maintenance | Has kept the change for more than six months | Support, identify high-risk situations, celebrate success |
| Termination | No temptation to return (not reached by everyone) | — |

**Relapse** to an earlier stage is common and is treated as part of the process, not a failure. The model is often drawn as a cycle or spiral.

**Processes of change** (how people move): consciousness raising, dramatic relief, self-re-evaluation, self-liberation (commitment), counter-conditioning (healthier substitutes), stimulus control (removing cues), reinforcement management (rewards), helping relationships.

**Decisional balance** (pros versus cons) and **self-efficacy** shift as people move through the stages.

### Motivational interviewing (MI)

A collaborative counselling style (William Miller and Stephen Rollnick) that strengthens a person's own motivation for change, especially useful in contemplation. Core skills, **OARS**:

- **O**pen questions — "What concerns you most about your smoking?"
- **A**ffirmations — "You've done well to cut down."
- **R**eflective listening — "You want to quit, but you're worried about the cravings."
- **S**ummarising.

MI avoids arguing; it draws out the patient's own reasons for change ("change talk").

### Practical strategies to improve adherence

1. Simplify the regimen (fewer daily doses, combination products where appropriate — decided by the prescriber).
2. Clear verbal and written instructions; teach-back.
3. Link doses to daily routines; pill organisers, blister calendar packs, alarms, SMS reminders.
4. Discuss and manage side effects.
5. Address beliefs and fears (HBM, CBT approach).
6. Match advice to the stage of change (TTM).
7. Involve family support.
8. Regular follow-up and refill reminders; praise progress (reinforcement).

## 5.5 Psychological first aid and crisis communication

### Psychological first aid (PFA)

**Psychological first aid** is humane, supportive, practical help for people who have recently suffered a serious crisis — disaster, accident, violence, sudden death of a loved one. It is not professional counselling or therapy and does not ask people to describe the event in detail. It can be given by any trained helper, including pharmacists.

**Aims:** safety, calm, connection, hope and self-efficacy.

The World Health Organization's guide describes three action principles:

| Principle | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| LOOK | Check for safety; check for people with urgent basic needs; look for people with serious distress reactions |
| LISTEN | Approach people who may need support; ask about needs and concerns; listen and help them feel calm |
| LINK | Help people meet basic needs and access services; help them cope with problems; give information; connect them with loved ones and social support |

**Do's:** be honest and trustworthy; respect the person's right to make decisions; be aware of your own biases; offer practical help (water, a phone, a quiet place); keep information confidential; respect culture.

**Don'ts:** don't pressure people to tell their story; don't give false promises; don't judge; don't think you must solve every problem; don't put yourself at risk.

**Normal reactions to crisis:** shock, fear, crying, anger, numbness, sleep problems, difficulty concentrating. Most people recover with support; refer those who cannot care for themselves, may harm themselves or others, or remain severely distressed.

### Crisis communication

**Crisis communication** is the communication used during emergencies — epidemics, disasters, drug recalls, contaminated products — to give the public accurate information quickly so they can protect themselves.

**Principles (crisis and emergency risk communication)**

1. **Be first** — information should come quickly.
2. **Be right** — accuracy builds credibility; say what is known, what is not known and what is being done.
3. **Be credible** — honesty and openness.
4. **Express empathy** — acknowledge fear and suffering.
5. **Promote action** — give simple, specific things people can do.
6. **Show respect.**

**Good practice:** one consistent message from a trusted spokesperson; simple language; repeat key messages; use several channels (TV, radio, SMS, social media, community leaders); correct rumours and misinformation quickly; update regularly. Experience during the COVID-19 pandemic showed how misinformation spreads quickly and how trusted local health workers, including pharmacists, can counter it.

**Pharmacist's role:** give accurate information about medicines and vaccines, counter rumours (false "miracle cures"), manage panic buying, communicate drug recalls, and support distressed people.

## 5.6 Mental health promotion and stigma reduction through communication

### Mental health

The World Health Organization describes mental health as a state of well-being in which a person realises their own abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and can contribute to the community. Mental health is more than the absence of mental illness.

**Mental health promotion** aims to strengthen well-being for everyone, not only to treat illness:

- Awareness campaigns (for example on World Mental Health Day, 10 October)
- Life-skills and stress-management education in schools and colleges
- Workplace mental health programmes
- Early recognition and referral
- Support for vulnerable groups (elderly, people with chronic disease, carers, students)
- Easy access to help — in India, the National Mental Health Programme (started 1982) and the Tele-MANAS tele-mental-health service

### Stigma

**Stigma** is a mark of disgrace attached to a person because of a characteristic — here, mental illness (also seen with HIV, tuberculosis, leprosy, epilepsy and substance use). Sociologist Erving Goffman described stigma as an attribute that discredits a person.

| Type of stigma | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Public (social) stigma | Negative attitudes of society: "mentally ill people are dangerous" |
| Self-stigma | The person believes the stereotypes about themselves and feels shame |
| Structural (institutional) stigma | Policies and systems that disadvantage people |
| Associative stigma | Stigma felt by family members and carers |

Components: stereotypes (beliefs) → prejudice (feelings) → discrimination (actions).

**Effects of stigma:** people hide symptoms, delay seeking help, stop medicines, lose jobs and relationships, feel isolated and hopeless.

### Reducing stigma through communication

**Three recognised strategies:**

1. **Education** — replacing myths with facts (mental illness is common and treatable; it is not a weakness or a curse).
2. **Contact** — meeting and hearing from people with lived experience of recovery; considered one of the most effective strategies.
3. **Protest / advocacy** — challenging stigmatising media portrayals and policies.

**Language matters — use person-first, respectful words**

| Avoid | Prefer |
| --- | --- |
| "a schizophrenic", "a diabetic" | "a person with schizophrenia", "a person with diabetes" |
| "mad", "mental", "psycho" | "a person with a mental health condition" |
| "committed suicide" | "died by suicide" |
| "suffering from", "victim of" | "living with", "has" |
| "addict" | "a person with a substance use disorder" |

**What a pharmacist can do**

- Treat every patient with mental illness with the same respect as any other.
- Counsel privately and without judgement about psychiatric medicines; explain that they take time to work and should not be stopped suddenly without advice.
- Correct myths ("these medicines are addictive", "you only need them when you feel bad").
- Recognise warning signs and refer; respond to suicidal talk seriously and connect the person to help.
- Display mental health information and helpline details.
- Support carers.

**Legal support in India:** the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 gives persons with mental illness the right to access mental healthcare, to be treated with dignity, to confidentiality and to protection from cruel treatment. It also states that a person who attempts suicide is presumed, unless proved otherwise, to have severe stress and is not to be punished, and directs the government to provide care to such persons.

## Remember

- HBM: perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, self-efficacy.
- Illness behaviour (Mechanic); Suchman's five stages; Parsons' sick role.
- Psychosomatic illness = real physical disease influenced by psychological factors; HPA axis and sympathetic system link stress to the body; placebo and nocebo.
- Adherence > compliance; non-adherence is primary, unintentional or intentional; WHO five dimensions.
- CBT: thoughts–feelings–behaviour triangle; ABC model; cognitive restructuring.
- TTM: precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (→ termination); relapse is normal; match advice to stage.
- Motivational interviewing uses OARS.
- PFA (WHO): Look, Listen, Link — not therapy, no forcing to talk.
- Crisis communication: be first, be right, be credible, show empathy, promote action, show respect.
- Stigma: public, self, structural; reduce through education, contact, advocacy and person-first language.
